units.translation: But for the stranger, an ancient wreath of willow, the best of bonds, from the story of Prometheus.
Of robes and wreaths, if not now, when shall we have them for our prayers?
To those who send these wreaths.

which the old scholiast explains by ἐπλήρουν [they filled], Thomas Magister by περιετίθουν [they placed around].
Crowned with the greatest fillet in a sober manner.
Respect the stern of the city thus crowned.
And memorials of themselves to their parents' homes, to the chariot of Adrastus, they crowned with their hands.

The tragedians are accustomed to use the plural στέρνα [breasts].
The word reaches through the breast.
I think that from their lovely deep-bosomed breasts they will send forth worthy grief.

For all the tatters of my embroidered garments are torn with broken threads around my body under the pain of evils.

The imperative is missing: hence Brunck indicated a lacuna after ἥλιοστιβεῖς [sun-trodden], from whom Hartung dissented and conjectured ήλίου στίβει [tread the sun] (preceded by I. Siebelis, who had proposed ἡλίου στιβεῖς [you tread the sun]) but kept περῶσα [crossing] in the next verse, for which Heimsoeth wrote παρεῖσα [letting pass] in the Bonn Program of March 1874 p. 12. But the present form usual among the ancients is στείβω [I tread], in manuscripts often written στίβω [I tread], as στίχω [I go] is written for στείχω [I go]. The form στιβέω [I tread], of which there are no examples, was posited by the grammarians indicated in the Thesaurus vol. 7 p. 764 on account of the perfect ἐστίβηται [has been trodden] in Sophocles Ai. 874 and the adjective ἀστίβητος [untrodden], which, as ἀστιβής [untrodden], formed from στείβω [I tread], Aeschylus used in Sept. 857: τὰν μελάγκροκον θεωρίδα, τὰν ἀστιβῆ ᾿πόλλωνι, τὰν ἀνάλιον [the black-robed procession, the untrodden one for Apollo, the sunless one]. The aorist στιβῆσαι [to tread] was invented by Eustathius p. 179, 35. 1035, 31. From these it follows that, if ἡλιοστιβεῖς [sun-trodden] is to be kept, one must return to Brunck's opinion and that ἀντολὰς ἡλιοστιβεῖς [sun-trodden risings] are permeated by the sun, as Todt translated in Comment. p. 41: unless, which would be most fitting of all, Aeschylus wrote πρὸς ἀντολὰς φλογῶπας ἡλίου στρέφου [turn toward the fiery risings of the sun], as above v. 707 he said πρῶτον μὲν ἐνθένδ᾽ ἡλίου πρὸς ἀντολὰς | στρέψασα σαυτὴν στεῖχ᾽ ἀνι ἀνηρότους γύας [first from here toward the risings of the sun, turning yourself, go up through the unplowed fields]. For if he wanted to use some imperative, no reason can be devised why he would prefer to invent an unheard-of form στίβει [tread] rather than write στρέφου [turn].
Toward the fiery sun-trodden risings, crossing the roar of the sea.
